constraints: A search may omit records appended during the last 60 seconds, but may not return a snapshot older than 60 seconds.
Results must remain isolated by tenant, effective permission scope and search parameters; current authorization is checked on every request.
The derived cache may be evicted or unavailable. A failed origin read must not turn an expired snapshot into a successful current result.
The optimization must share repeated search work across devices. Browser and edge layers do not have validated permission context.

feedback.details:
The ledger remains the authority for durable audit writes; the cache stores a disposable read projection. After checking current authorization, the audit service looks up a key containing tenant, effective permission scope and normalized search parameters. It measures snapshot age from the source read, including any upstream delay, rather than restarting the age on a cache hit. A result within the 60-second bound can be reused; an expired or missing result requires a fresh ledger read or successful source validation before reuse. Permission changes must affect the authorization check and effective scope on the next request.

For a snapshot read at 10:00:00, a request at 10:00:40 may omit a record appended at 10:00:30. At 10:01:01 that snapshot is too old: refresh it, or report the read unavailable if the source cannot provide a valid result. A timestamp does not relax the bound. An edge key based only on a URL can leak results across callers, and private browser copies do not share work across devices. Cache persistence is not the audit retention guarantee. If the product instead required every newly appended record immediately, this time-bounded reuse policy would be insufficient; source validation or a stronger coherence rule would be needed.

messages.text: The same URL can be requested by different tenants or permission scopes. Authorizing only cache fills allows later hits to bypass current authorization.
Private browser copies may isolate local results, but they do not share repeated search work across analyst devices as required by this workload.
The expired snapshot exceeds the read contract even when labeled with a timestamp. Origin failure must produce an unavailable read instead of a successful stale result.
A disposable read cache cannot acknowledge the durable audit-write obligation. The ledger must remain the write authority; this optimization concerns repeated reads.

feedback.reason: The service can both validate the current caller and share correctly scoped read results across devices. The 60-second freshness bound permits derived reuse, but does not permit serving an expired snapshot or transferring audit durability to the cache.

options.text: Cache search responses at the edge for 60 seconds using the request URL as the key. Authenticate at the service only when filling a missing entry.
Cache derived search results in the audit service by tenant, permission scope and query. Check authorization and age on every request; refresh expired results from the ledger.
Cache search responses privately in each browser for 60 seconds and ask the service to authorize every cache read. Let each device reuse only its own entries.
Cache tenant- and permission-scoped results in the service for 60 seconds. If a ledger read fails after expiry, serve the older snapshot with its timestamp.
Make the service cache acknowledge audit appends and retain entries for the audit obligation. Read searches there and copy accepted writes into the ledger asynchronously.

prompt: Analysts repeatedly search a tenant-scoped audit ledger from several devices. The audit service checks current permissions on every search and is the only layer with validated tenant and permission context. The ledger already owns durable, attributable writes. Which cache placement best reduces repeated search reads while preserving the stated read contract?

constraints: The user is signed in and the client knows the authenticated account.
Five minutes of staleness is acceptable for this screen.
The cache is for repeated reads on one device; writes remain server-owned.

feedback.details:
The cache belongs at the client because repeated reads are local and cross-device sharing is unnecessary. Scope it to the authenticated account and discard it at account change; the five-minute bound controls how long the screen may reuse it. Sending edits to the service preserves one write owner. A shared edge is not safe merely because the URL is stable, and a durable client-only record cannot satisfy the service’s role for other devices. If the UI later promises immediate cross-device preference visibility, this placement would need a shared validated read path or shorter freshness bound.

Boundary and reversal: If preferences become security-sensitive or must change across devices immediately, stop reusing this client copy until the stronger authorization and freshness requirements are satisfied.

messages.text: The key does not isolate user-specific preferences.
The cache becomes a second write authority, so other devices and server workflows can diverge.

feedback.reason: A private device cache meets the stated single-device reuse and five-minute freshness needs while keeping the service authoritative for writes. A shared URL key could mix users, and local-only writes would create a second authority.

options.text: Keep a private five-minute preference copy keyed to the signed-in account; send edits through the preference service.
Cache by URL at a shared edge and reuse the response for all callers for five minutes.
Treat the device copy as authoritative and accept preference changes locally without synchronizing the service.

prompt: A notification screen reads a user’s preferences repeatedly. They are low sensitivity, may be up to five minutes stale, and do not need to be shared between devices; writes still go to the preference service.

constraints: A parcel projection and each update notification carry the same monotonically increasing parcel revision.
The origin can return the latest committed projection and its revision on a new read.
The cache must keep reusing unchanged parcel projections rather than send every read to the origin.

feedback.details:
Before returning a successful ACK, publish the committed revision floor to the cache read path and remove any older entry. A refresh that began earlier may still finish, so deletion alone is insufficient: reject any fill below the visible floor. A subsequent read can then fetch the latest committed projection at or above that revision. Waiting for expiry violates the post-acknowledgement read requirement. The origin-reuse premise rules out bypassing the cache on every read.

Boundary and reversal: If projections and notifications cannot be compared by revision, do not claim read-after-acknowledgement; use an explicit unavailable or bounded-stale contract.

messages.text: An older in-flight fill can repopulate the entry after the update has been acknowledged.
The next read could remain stale for the rest of the 20-second lifetime.

feedback.reason: The notification establishes a revision floor. Rejecting a fill below that floor prevents an older in-flight read from undoing the acknowledged update.

options.text: Install the revision floor on the cache read path before ACK; reject older fills and serve only data at or above it.
Delete the current entry on update, but allow an already-running older read to refill it afterward.
Keep the cached projection until its 20-second lifetime expires, then refresh from origin.

prompt: A tracking service caches each parcel projection. Reads may be in flight when a tracking update commits, and an older read can finish after the update notification. After the update is acknowledged, the next read must show that committed state.

constraints: The file has a stable content digest.
The extractor version is recorded with every result.
Results must not be shared across tenant boundaries.

feedback.details:
The processor can reuse an immutable derived artifact because the input and transformation are fixed. The tenant component prevents one tenant’s cache entry from satisfying another tenant’s request, the digest identifies the bytes, and the extractor version distinguishes changed transformations. A filename is not content identity, and a job ID identifies an attempt rather than reusable work. This design assumes the result itself remains within the tenant boundary; if extracted data has additional user-level permissions, include that scope or reauthorize before returning it.

Boundary and reversal: If extraction becomes nondeterministic or depends on an external reference not captured in the key, either add that input to the key or stop reusing the result.

messages.text: Names can collide, tenant data can leak, and the result may come from old processing logic.
This key cannot identify deterministic work shared by repeated inputs.

feedback.reason: Tenant, content digest and extractor version together identify a reusable result. Omitting tenant risks cross-tenant disclosure; omitting the version can serve output produced by different logic.

options.text: Cache the immutable result by tenant, content digest, and extractor version; reuse only when all three match.
Cache globally by filename and reuse the result regardless of tenant or extractor release.
Cache only by job ID, so every repeat upload creates a new key and repeats extraction.

prompt: A document processor receives identical files more than once. Extraction output is deterministic for a given file and extractor version, but files are tenant-private and a new extractor release can change results.

constraints: A layout is immutable within a published venue-layout version.
The origin cannot serve the repeated static layout traffic directly.
Availability changes independently and must be fetched from its authority for each display.

feedback.details:
Cache only the immutable layout artifact, using venue and published layout version as its identity. Read current availability from the availability owner for each display because sales can change it without a layout release. Combining those values makes the exact, mutable part stale; bypassing layout reuse sends traffic to an origin that cannot serve it. This is a cache-placement and data-separation decision, not a claim that the cached layout reserves seats. If the product later accepts bounded-stale availability, it can define a separate estimate cache without changing the layout contract.

Boundary and reversal: If the availability service later allows a documented freshness window, a separate availability projection may be cached within that bound; it must remain independent from the immutable seat-map artifact.

messages.text: Sales change availability without changing the layout version.
The origin cannot serve the repeated layout traffic, and the layout is safely reusable by version.

feedback.reason: Versioning gives the static layout a stable shared identity, while current availability has a separate owner and must not inherit that cache lifetime.

options.text: Cache layout by venue/version; read availability live on each display.
Cache layout and availability together under venue ID until the next layout release.
Fetch both layout and availability from origin for every display.

prompt: A ticket page serves a venue seat map and current seat availability. Layout changes only by published layout version; availability changes after every sale and must be exact when displayed. The origin limits layout downloads, but availability can be fetched from its owning service.

constraints: Candidate IDs can be shared within one tenant.
Case-level authorization differs by agent and can change immediately.
The case service can authorize each candidate before returning its contents.

feedback.details:
Cache only the candidate identifiers under tenant and normalized query. Before returning any document, the case service checks the current agent’s rights; a cached ID cannot itself grant access. Caching the final document by tenant incorrectly assumes all agents share permissions. Keying by agent without a permission-version check or bounded invalidation still serves content after rights change. If the index itself contains sensitive snippets, even candidate caching needs narrower access controls; the scenario explicitly makes IDs shareable within the tenant.

Boundary and reversal: If the search index cannot safely expose candidate IDs across agents, scope candidate caching to the agent or move filtering into the authorized search boundary.

messages.text: Tenant membership alone does not grant every agent the same case access.
A permission change leaves the old result eligible for that agent.

feedback.reason: The search candidate set is reusable within a tenant, but disclosure is agent-specific and must be checked on each response. Caching IDs and reauthorizing content separates those two boundaries.

options.text: Cache tenant/query candidate IDs; fetch each case and authorize it for the current agent.
Cache the final case documents by tenant and query and reuse them for any agent in that tenant.
Cache final results by agent ID with no permission-version check or expiry.

prompt: Support search spans cases within a tenant. Agents have different case permissions, and permission changes must take effect on the next response; the search index can return candidate IDs separately from case content.

constraints: The metadata is public and identical for all viewers.
The maximum stale age is 15 seconds.
The origin limits full transfers to one per URL per 15 seconds and supports conditional validation.

feedback.details:
The 15-second value belongs to the cache’s freshness policy for this mutable URL. Once it expires, the validator lets the edge ask whether the stored representation is still current and avoid retransferring unchanged bytes. The validator does not make an expired copy fresh by itself; the origin’s validation response does that. A long TTL plus hoped-for purges cannot guarantee the stated bound, and unconditional full fetches waste an available validation path. If the origin cannot be reached after expiry, the edge must follow an explicitly allowed stale-if-error policy; none is given here.

Boundary and reversal: If the product explicitly allows stale serving during origin failure, add a maximum stale-on-error window and expose that behavior; do not infer it from the normal 15-second bound.

messages.text: The given bound would depend on a best-effort invalidation reaching every location.
This discards conditional validation even though the origin can confirm an unchanged representation.

feedback.reason: A short freshness lifetime controls how long an edge may reuse the mutable copy without checking. After that, conditional revalidation can establish whether the stored representation remains current.

options.text: Cache for 15 seconds, then conditionally revalidate the origin before reuse.
Cache the mutable URL for a day and assume a purge will always reach each edge within 15 seconds.
Fetch a complete representation from origin on every request and ignore the supplied validator.

prompt: A media catalog serves a mutable public metadata URL worldwide. Titles can change several times a day, edge copies may be no more than 15 seconds stale, and the origin supplies a validator. The origin permits at most one full representation transfer per URL in each 15-second window; conditional validation is allowed.

constraints: A manifest is immutable for a model and firmware build.
Operational state is per-device and can change without a firmware change.
The portal can request manifest and operational state separately.

feedback.details:
A firmware build identifies the supported capabilities; the model alone may cover multiple builds. Cache that manifest broadly under both dimensions. Keep live connectivity and reported state on the device service path because two devices on the same build can differ, and a state change does not create a new manifest. Combining them lets a long-lived capability cache freeze operational facts. If a firmware build can change capabilities after publication, the manifest is not immutable and needs its own revision or revalidation rule.

Boundary and reversal: If the portal only needs a historic “last known state,” it can cache that separately with a timestamp and explicit age label; the current view described here must use live state.

messages.text: Capabilities can differ between firmware builds of the same model.
One device’s changing connectivity state is neither shared by model nor immutable.

feedback.reason: The manifest is shared and immutable only within a model/build pair. Device connectivity has a different owner and freshness requirement, so it must not inherit the manifest cache lifetime.

options.text: Cache manifests by model/build; fetch live device state separately.
Cache one manifest per model and keep using it after devices move to a different firmware build.
Cache manifest and connectivity together by model for the manifest lifetime.

prompt: A device portal displays supported features and protocol limits. Those capabilities are identical for devices on the same firmware build and do not change after release; connectivity and reported state are device-specific and can change at any moment.

constraints: The local draft must survive a refresh on the same device.
The client can retain the server revision read before going offline.
Conflicting edits must not silently overwrite the server version.

feedback.details:
Keep the draft and its base revision together. After reconnection, submit with that version as a precondition; if the server has advanced, preserve the local draft and ask the user to merge rather than overwriting. The local cache is appropriate because the requirement is same-device recovery. It must not become a second shared authority, and discarding it loses work. If the editor supports automatic merges, apply its documented merge algorithm only after detecting the concurrent version.

Boundary and reversal: If the product explicitly chooses last-write-wins for this document type, it can omit conflict UI, but that would replace the stated no-silent-overwrite requirement.

messages.text: Offline state may be older than another collaborator’s saved revision.
The explicit refresh/offline requirement is not met.

feedback.reason: The client cache protects unsent work, while the saved base revision allows the server to detect a conflict before publication. Local persistence is not evidence that the shared document is current.

options.text: Keep the draft and base revision locally; submit conditionally after reconnect and show a conflict if changed.
Treat the local draft cache as the latest shared document and overwrite the server after reconnect.
Never retain a local copy and require the user to keep the page open until connectivity returns.

prompt: A document editor must survive browser refresh while offline. The server remains authoritative, and another collaborator may edit the same document before this client reconnects.

constraints: The road graph is immutable within a published release.
Live closure data has a 30-second maximum age.
A route reviewer must be able to verify the graph release and the closure observation time from each preview.

feedback.details:
Build the route from separately identified inputs. Region plus graph release ID selects an immutable topology artifact, while closure observations refresh under the 30-second bound. The response must return the graph release ID and the closure-observation timestamp so a reviewer can verify both inputs. A single route cache keyed only by endpoints omits those dimensions and can conceal new restrictions. Fetching graph tiles on every call does not solve stale closure data if the response omits its observation time.

Boundary and reversal: If live restrictions must take effect faster than 30 seconds, tighten that source’s bound or add an authoritative route-validation step; do not shorten the immutable graph cache for that purpose.

messages.text: A changed graph release or a new closure can make the cached route unsafe.
A route reviewer could not verify whether the changing closure input met its 30-second freshness bound.

feedback.reason: The graph release is safe to reuse by region and version; live closures are not. Keeping their cache lifetimes and timestamps separate prevents a current restriction from being hidden by a static topology cache.

options.text: Cache graph by region and release ID; refresh closures within 30 seconds and return the release ID plus closure-observation timestamp.
Cache a complete route with graph and closure assumptions for a day using only the origin and destination as key.
Fetch the graph each time, but omit the closure observation time from the route preview.

prompt: A route planner reads road topology and traffic restrictions from separate sources. Topology changes only in versioned releases, while closures may change every minute and must be reflected in previews within 30 seconds.

constraints: Forecast output depends on selected facility set, time horizon, and forecast-rule revision.
A live calculation takes 45 seconds; the planner response limit is two seconds.
Stock movement is incorporated in ten-minute batches, and the result must identify which batch it includes.

feedback.details:
Normalize the facility set and horizon into the cache key and include the rule revision because it changes the computation. Refresh the materialized result as new stock movement batches are incorporated; its watermark says which batch is represented. A generic report-name key silently mixes different planner questions, while live recomputation repeats the expensive aggregation and still cannot explain which rules version produced it. The two-second response bound rules out a fresh 45-second computation on each request; the watermark records the stock batch represented. This read model does not authorize a stock pick.

Boundary and reversal: If planners require a forecast based on a specific later watermark, wait for that source watermark or return that it is not yet available instead of relabeling an older result.

messages.text: Different planner requests and rule versions can receive the wrong aggregate.
A 45-second live calculation misses the two-second response limit, and the result would omit which rules revision produced it.

feedback.reason: The forecast is a reusable derived report only when its dimensions and rules match. Its watermark communicates stock-data progress independently of the cache age.

options.text: Key by facility set, horizon, and rule revision; refresh per stock batch and return its watermark.
Reuse the latest forecast under one shared report name regardless of facilities, horizon or rule revision.
Recompute from every facility’s live movements for each planner request and omit the rules revision from the result.

prompt: A warehouse planner needs a forecast over selected facilities and a time horizon. The computation takes 45 seconds, but the page must respond within two seconds; many planners request the same report. Stock batches arrive every ten minutes, and forecast rules can change independently.

constraints: Course outline content is public and immutable within a release.
Progress belongs to one learner and changes on completion.
Each page open must resolve the course URL to the currently published release; progress can be requested separately.

feedback.details:
Split the response at the data boundary. A public outline is immutable for a release, so its release ID is a safe shared cache key. Progress is learner-specific and mutable, so it must be retrieved under the current identity and must not ride in a course-wide cache entry. Caching the combined payload by course ID would leak or misstate progress. Avoiding all caching is unnecessary for the public part. If the course outline itself becomes personalized, it must leave the shared cache or include the personalization scope in its key.

Boundary and reversal: If progress has a documented local freshness allowance, the app may add a private learner-scoped cache with that explicit bound; none is specified here.

messages.text: The cache mixes one learner’s private state with another learner’s response.
The alias can move while release IDs remain immutable, so it does not identify one outline version.

feedback.reason: The two payloads have different owners and sharing rules. The immutable outline can be shared by release ID; learner progress must be fetched through its authorized path.

options.text: Cache the course outline by immutable release ID; fetch progress from the learner service under the current identity.
Cache the combined outline-and-progress response by course ID and reuse it for all learners.
Cache the outline by human-readable course URL across a release change, and keep the old outline under that alias.

prompt: A learning app serves the same course outline to every learner, but completion progress is private and changes after each saved lesson. Course releases have immutable version IDs, and the human-readable course URL can move to a newer release.

constraints: Published price revisions are immutable and public.
The browsing pointer may lag 15 seconds.
Checkout can revalidate the revision before accepting payment.

feedback.details:
Browsing and buying have different guarantees. The edge can cache a revision that never changes and resolve the current pointer within its 15-second limit. The checkout service then checks that the quote’s revision is still effective before accepting payment, so a stale browse response cannot silently charge the wrong current price. Depending on purge propagation as the only correctness mechanism overstates what the system knows. If the business honors any shown price even after publication changes, checkout’s revalidation policy must reflect that contractual promise instead.

Boundary and reversal: If the merchant contract guarantees the displayed price for a quote lifetime, checkout should validate that quote’s pinned revision rather than require the latest catalog revision.

messages.text: A stale edge copy can set the accepted payment amount beyond the allowed 15-second browse lag.
The scenario states only a bounded pointer lag, not a globally synchronous purge guarantee.

feedback.reason: Immutable revision URLs support safe edge reuse, while the mutable listing pointer has the stated 15-second bound. Checkout must still verify the effective revision before accepting payment.

options.text: Cache immutable prices by revision; bound the pointer to 15 seconds and revalidate at checkout.
Cache one mutable product URL for hours and let checkout accept whichever price the edge returns.
Assume every edge purge completes before publication succeeds and skip checkout revalidation.

prompt: A merchant publishes product prices to a global catalog. Browsing may show a price pointer that is 15 seconds old, but checkout must reject a quote if the effective price changed before acceptance.

constraints: The authoritative identity store reflects a revocation immediately; authorization reads do not use a lagging replica.
A protected request must be rejected within five seconds after revocation commit.
If current credential state is unavailable, the protected request must not be authorized.

feedback.details:
If the system caches credential status, the maximum age and invalidation path must fit within the five-second bound. On expiry or source failure, the service cannot know that the credential is still active, so it rejects or defers the protected operation according to its error contract. A long positive cache leaves revoked credentials usable; fail-open behavior makes a dependency outage an authorization decision. This may reduce availability, which is the explicit consequence of the requirement. If the product chooses a longer revocation window, state that policy change rather than silently extending cache TTL.

Boundary and reversal: If the operation is non-sensitive and the product explicitly allows bounded stale authorization, define that separate exception and do not apply it to the protected operation in this scenario.

messages.text: A credential revoked during that hour remains usable beyond the stated bound.
This turns unknown state into permission despite the fail-closed requirement.

feedback.reason: The cache lifetime cannot exceed the five-second revocation objective, and a lookup failure must not grant access. A longer positive cache would violate the stated limit.

options.text: Cache status for at most five seconds; deny when freshness is unknown.
Cache active status for an hour and continue accepting requests while the identity service is down.
On status lookup failure treat the credential as active to preserve availability.

prompt: An identity directory checks whether a credential is active. Its authoritative store reflects revocations immediately; authorization reads do not use a lagging replica. A protected request must be rejected within five seconds after the revocation is committed.

constraints: Each source file has a content digest.
The full encoding recipe and codec version are recorded.
Published outputs are immutable and public.

feedback.details:
Include the source digest, codec implementation version, resolution and every output-affecting setting in the key. A changed input or recipe creates a new immutable artifact instead of mutating a shared URL. Because these renditions are public, a CDN can reuse the artifact; the workflow’s job status remains a separate resource from the output. Caching by asset name risks collisions across source replacements, and returning a cached submission response does not supply completed content. If outputs contain private overlays, the public-cache assumption no longer holds.

Boundary and reversal: If the encoder is nondeterministic or depends on uncaptured data, include the missing input or stop treating the result as content-addressable.

messages.text: A replacement source or changed recipe can collide with the old artifact.
An accepted job record is not the immutable output bytes.

feedback.reason: The output identity must include the source content and the full transformation recipe. An immutable result can then be shared safely; asset name or job ID alone cannot identify its bytes.

options.text: Key by source digest and full encoding recipe; publish the output immutably.
Cache by asset name alone and overwrite the cached output when a worker finishes.
Cache the job submission response and return it as if it were the completed rendition.

prompt: A media workflow stores public renditions produced from source files. Outputs are deterministic for a fixed source digest, codec version, resolution and encoding settings; source replacements must become visible as new outputs.

constraints: The configuration is identical across callers and is safe to share.
After its 15-second freshness window, an old enabled value must not be used if revalidation fails.
The origin caps revalidation to one request per key per 15-second window.

feedback.details:
Because the configuration is public and identical across callers, the edge can hold one shared value per key during its freshness window. After 15 seconds, a revalidation is needed; if the origin is unavailable, the worker treats the feature as disabled rather than using the old enabled value. Request coalescing at the key boundary respects the origin’s one-request budget. This is a cache-freshness and failure decision, not an assertion that push invalidation is reliable. If configuration were secret or tenant-specific, the sharing scope would change.

Boundary and reversal: If a faster emergency-disable objective is needed, state it separately and support it with a verified invalidation path; the 15-second freshness window does not imply a stronger guarantee.

messages.text: This exceeds the origin limit of one revalidation per key in each 15-second window.
An expired value is explicitly unusable when revalidation fails.

feedback.reason: A shared value can be reused for 15 seconds, but expiry requires one bounded revalidation and failure disables the feature. Neither repeated origin reads nor stale enabled reuse meets the stated constraints.

options.text: Cache 15 seconds, revalidate once after expiry, and disable on failure.
Bypass the cache and query the origin for every edge request, even when the current value is still fresh.
Continue serving an expired enabled value during a prolonged origin outage and revalidate in the background.

prompt: Edge workers read a public, non-secret feature configuration. A value may be reused for at most 15 seconds; after expiry an unavailable origin means the feature must be treated as disabled. The origin allows at most one revalidation request per key during each 15-second window.

constraints: The calendar is a read-only availability projection.
Schedule changes normally invalidate affected provider/time-window entries.
The booking service can recheck and claim a slot atomically.

feedback.details:
Build the read cache around the schedule dimensions that determine its contents: provider and time window. An update can evict affected entries early, while the 30-second maximum age remains the fallback if invalidation is delayed. On confirmation, the booking service checks current schedule state and creates the booking atomically. A cached open slot is not a hold. A global cache key erases the provider and time context, and a cache-as-lock can admit conflicting requests. If the product wants to hold a slot during checkout, create a separate expiring hold with an authoritative identity.

Boundary and reversal: If the business promises that a displayed slot is reserved for a user, add a durable expiring-hold contract instead of treating the availability cache as a reservation.

messages.text: Two users can act on the same stale open-slot result.
The key merges distinct schedules and cannot identify which change should invalidate it.

feedback.reason: A bounded projection is useful for browsing, but only the booking authority can claim a slot. Provider/window keys permit targeted invalidation, and the atomic recheck protects the no-overlap invariant.

options.text: Cache by provider/window for 30 seconds; evict on change and claim atomically at booking.
Treat an open slot in the cache as a reservation and confirm it without checking the booking record.
Cache one availability response for all providers and time windows because the display may be stale.

prompt: A calendar screen shows open appointment slots for a provider. The display may be 30 seconds old, booking changes emit an invalidation event, and a confirmed booking must never overlap another confirmed booking for that provider.

constraints: The response is public and identical for the same normalized query and locale.
At most one origin refresh may run for a cache key at a time.
A previously computed result may be served until it is 20 seconds old while one refresh is in progress.

feedback.details:
Normalize query and locale before constructing the key, then maintain one in-flight refresh for that key. Concurrent callers can await its result or receive the prior response if it remains inside the stated 20-second window. The key must not collapse distinct searches, and starting one computation per caller would exceed the origin limit during a traffic spike. This item concerns duplicate-work control for a read-only result; it does not claim a snapshot across multiple search pages or a source watermark. If the prior result is older than 20 seconds and refresh fails, return the defined unavailable outcome rather than extending its age silently.

Boundary and reversal: If each request carries caller-specific filters or authorization, include those dimensions in the key or avoid sharing the response; the scenario only permits sharing a public normalized query.

messages.text: This violates the one-refresh-per-key limit and multiplies the expensive work.
Different normalized queries can have different results and cannot share one cache key.

feedback.reason: Per-key coalescing respects the origin’s single-refresh limit while the 20-second age bound permits concurrent readers to receive the last result during refresh.

options.text: Key by normalized query/locale; coalesce one refresh and serve the prior result for at most 20 seconds.
Start a separate origin computation for every simultaneous request, even when query and locale match.
Use one shared result for every query and locale until any request triggers a refresh.

prompt: A public trending-search query is expensive to compute. Identical requests for the same normalized query and locale often arrive together; the service permits one refresh per key at a time and allows a result to be up to 20 seconds old.
